common_name: Rutgers Beacon Asparagus (Early Rutgers Polycross Hybrid)

planting.note: Set crowns into a 6-8 inch deep trench as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, backfilling progressively through the season.

directions: Rutgers Beacon is an early dioecious asparagus hybrid developed at the Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station, part of the university's long-running asparagus breeding program that later produced the all-male Jersey series. Unlike the all-male supermale hybrids bred afterward, Rutgers Beacon includes both male and female plants, so some volunteer seedlings can appear in an established bed over time. It was grown across the Midwest and East Coast for its solid field performance before being largely superseded by higher-yielding all-male hybrids, and its male lines were themselves used as breeding stock for later Rutgers supermale releases such as Eros, Atlas, and Apollo. Give crowns two full seasons to establish before harvesting, then cut spears daily during the spring flush to keep the plant signaling new growth.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station
New Zealand Journal of Experimental Agriculture

common_name: Katharine Fay Iris (Historic White Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with the top surface exposed to the sun in late summer to early fall; Katharine Fay is a 1943 Orville Fay tall bearded iris grown today mainly for its place in white-iris breeding history.

directions: Katharine Fay is a tall bearded iris registered by hybridizer Orville Fay in 1943, valued today mainly as a foundational white-flowered parent in Fay's breeding program rather than as a widely grown garden plant in its own right. Its clean white standards and falls earned early recognition, including an American Iris Society Honorable Mention in 1945 and an Award of Merit in 1947, at a time when true white tall bearded irises were still relatively uncommon. Fay crossed Katharine Fay with 'Snow Flurry' to produce the more famous 'New Snow,' passing its pure white color into later generations of white bearded iris. Plant rhizomes shallowly with the top exposed to full sun in well-drained soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant after last frost on a sturdy overhead trellis in full sun; this is a dioecious vine requiring a compatible male Actinidia chinensis vine nearby for fruit set.

directions: Zespri SunGold, registered under the cultivar name 'Zesy002', was selected by the Zespri and Plant & Food Research breeding program in New Zealand from a cross made around 2000 at Te Puke and released to growers in the early 2010s as a hardier, more disease-tolerant replacement for the original gold kiwifruit variety, 'Hort16A', which had been devastated by bacterial canker (Psa). The smooth, hairless, bronze-gold skin lacks the pointed beak of its predecessor and often shows a faint pink to red blush around the stem end, surrounding sweet, golden-yellow flesh that is markedly less acidic than green kiwifruit and notably high in vitamin C. Because Zespri holds exclusive commercial rights and licenses SunGold vines only to contracted growers within its marketing system, home gardeners generally cannot legally obtain true 'Zesy002' vines outside that licensed network, unlike most other gold kiwi cultivars. Where it is grown commercially, it follows standard golden kiwifruit culture: a sturdy overhead trellis, a compatible male pollinator vine, and open pruning to maximize airflow and reduce Psa pressure.
sources: New Zealand Journal of Crop and Horticultural Science
